title: Build an audit evidence collector
description: A system that gathers audit evidence from your systems, maps it to the control it satisfies, and keeps a folder ready before your next audit.

api.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
api.content: A way for two programs to talk to each other. When a tool says 'connect via API,' it means software can send requests and get data back automatically — no manual copy-paste needed.

pull.title: Pull
pull.content: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your computer so your local copy is up to date. Claude pulls before starting work to make sure it's building on the newest version, not an old one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

automation.title: Automation
automation.content: Having Claude run tasks automatically on a schedule or trigger — without you manually starting them each time. For example, checking your inbox every morning and summarizing it to Slack.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Audit evidence doesn't gather itself. [Vanta reports](https://vanta.com/resources/automated-evidence-collection-for-compliance-all-you-need-to-know) that automated evidence collection cuts manual compliance work by 50 hours a month, and the same approach runs more than 1,200 compliance tests hourly against connected systems, a pace no one screenshotting dashboards by hand can match. A single SOC 2 audit alone can call for more than 150 distinct pieces of evidence pulled from a dozen or more systems, per industry reporting on SOC 2 evidence scope.

This system pulls current evidence for a named set of controls, maps each piece to the specific control it satisfies, and files everything into an audit-ready folder, instead of chasing it down system by system every cycle.

Run it as a one-time paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) ahead of an audit, a saved skill you run every cycle, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that keeps the folder current between audits. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your source systems.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your control set, your evidence sources, your refresh cadence per control, and what an audit-ready folder should contain.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that gathers recurring audit evidence, maps each piece to the control it satisfies, and keeps it organized ahead of our next audit. Ask me questions, one at a time, about which controls we're tracking, where the underlying evidence actually lives across our systems, how often each piece needs to be refreshed, and what an auditor expects to see when they open the folder. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces where evidence lives across your systems before you build, and the scope document becomes the brief for every collection run after it.

items: Which systems hold the evidence for each control.
Your refresh cadence per control, since access lists go stale faster than a signed policy.
Who reviews the collected evidence before an auditor sees it.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are a compliance [automation](#tooltip-automation) platform (Vanta, Drata) if you have one, your identity and access system (Okta, Google Workspace), and your cloud provider's console or [API](#tooltip-api) (AWS, Azure, GCP). The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build the system your scope document describes, and test it on your actual control set. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document gives you a version for your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Collect current evidence for [our named control set, e.g. SOC 2 access-control and change-management controls], map each piece to its control, and organize it into an audit-ready folder structure.

Context: [Paste our controls and their evidence requirements, our named evidence sources such as an IAM tool, ticketing system, or cloud config, and our last audit's evidence folder for reference on expected format.]

Rules:
- Map every piece of evidence to a specific named control, never a vague "compliance" bucket.
- Timestamp every collected item so staleness is visible at a glance.
- If evidence for a control can't be located or looks outdated, flag it explicitly rather than leaving a silent gap.
- Never fabricate or infer evidence that wasn't actually pulled from the source system.
- Output as one folder per control area, with each file named by control ID and collection date, plus a summary index of what's covered and what's missing.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the control set and timestamping every item keeps gaps visible instead of a folder that looks complete but quietly missed something.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every control mapped, timestamps present, gaps flagged instead of hidden?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Build a staleness alert that flags evidence approaching its re-check date before an audit forces the issue.
Extend collection to a second framework once the first control set is solid.
Add a control-mapping matrix that shows coverage gaps across frameworks at a glance.
Automate the summary index an auditor sees first.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft a rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each collection run, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, controls covered, evidence flagged missing or stale, false gaps, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make recurring gaps visible after a few runs.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few runs straight, package the prompt, control mapping, and folder structure into a reusable AI skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. Automated collection can quietly keep [pulling](#tooltip-pull) evidence for a control that's since changed, giving false confidence that a gap is covered. Review the control-to-evidence mapping itself on a schedule. Checking only the freshness of what's collected won't catch it.
